scenarios.title: Is OpenShift just Kubernetes?
scenarios.situation: A developer says 'OpenShift is just Kubernetes with a logo — I can use plain kubectl and YAML and ignore the rest.' Their first deploy fails on security constraints they never hit on vanilla K8s.
scenarios.prompt: What does OpenShift add on top of Kubernetes, and what bit them?
choices: Opinionated defaults: projects, Routes, Builds, ImageStreams, and Security Context Constraints — the SCC 'restricted' default likely blocked their container running as root
Nothing — OpenShift is byte-for-byte identical to upstream Kubernetes
Only a web console — the CLI and APIs are identical with no behavioral differences
OpenShift removes Kubernetes networking — that's why the deploy failed
scenarios.why: OpenShift is Kubernetes plus an opinionated platform layer: SCCs (admission control on pod security — containers don't run as root by default), Routes for external access, BuildConfigs/ImageStreams for image workflows, and Operators managing the platform itself. kubectl works, but oc exposes the OpenShift-native resources, and SCCs are the classic surprise for K8s veterans.
scenarios.hint: What admits or rejects a Pod based on its security context before it runs?

scenarios.title: Projects vs namespaces
scenarios.situation: You run 'oc new-project team-a' and a teammate says 'that's just a namespace — why not kubectl create namespace?'
scenarios.prompt: What does a project add beyond a namespace?
choices: A namespace plus OpenShift annotations (display name, description, requester) and automatic RBAC/policy setup — the API object is still a Namespace underneath
A completely separate cluster per project
Projects bypass all RBAC — anyone can create them
Nothing — oc new-project is an alias with no additional behavior
scenarios.why: A Project is a Kubernetes Namespace with extra metadata annotations and self-service provisioning: creating one also sets up default RBAC roles, quotas hooks, and network policy defaults per cluster configuration. 'oc projects' lists the ones you can access. Underneath, it's a Namespace — kubectl sees it too.
scenarios.hint: What does the API server actually store when you create a project?

scenarios.title: Exposing the app
scenarios.situation: On vanilla K8s you'd create an Ingress. On OpenShift, 'oc expose svc/frontend' creates something else, and external traffic works immediately with no ingress controller to install.
scenarios.prompt: What did oc expose create, and why does it work out of the box?
choices: A Route — OpenShift ships a default HAProxy-based router (Ingress Operator) in every cluster, so Routes work without extra installation
An Ingress — oc expose is just an alias for kubectl's ingress creation
A LoadBalancer Service — OpenShift auto-provisions cloud load balancers
A NodePort — external traffic hits node ports directly
scenarios.why: Routes are OpenShift's native external-access object, served by the built-in router (HAProxy, managed by the Ingress Operator). 'oc expose' creates one with an admitted hostname automatically. OpenShift also supports standard Ingress, but Routes predate it and add features like edge/passthrough/re-encrypt TLS termination modes.
scenarios.hint: Which component is already running in every OpenShift cluster to serve external HTTP?

scenarios.title: SSH to the node to install a package?
scenarios.situation: A node needs a debugging tool. You SSH in, run yum install, and it works — but after the next Machine Config Operator rollout, the package is gone.
scenarios.prompt: Why, and what is the correct way to change node configuration?
choices: Worker nodes run immutable RHEL CoreOS — manual changes are wiped; node config must go through MachineConfig objects applied by the MCO
yum is broken on CoreOS — you must use rpm-ostree install instead
The package was removed by a cron job — disable the cron
SSH is disabled on OpenShift nodes — you imagined the session
scenarios.why: RHEL CoreOS is an immutable container-optimized OS: /usr is read-only and the system is managed as a unit. The Machine Config Operator applies MachineConfig CRs (files, systemd units, kernel args) across machine pools, draining and rebooting nodes in a controlled rollout. Manual SSH tweaks are intentionally ephemeral — the MCO reverts drift.
scenarios.hint: Who owns the desired state of the nodes' operating systems?

scenarios.title: Who runs the platform?
scenarios.situation: You notice the cluster's etcd, DNS, and ingress are all managed by things called 'operators' rather than static manifests or systemd units.
scenarios.prompt: What is the operator pattern, and why does OpenShift use it for platform components?
choices: Operators extend the API with CRDs plus controllers that reconcile desired state in a loop — encoding operational knowledge (upgrades, backups, scaling) as software
Operators are just a new name for DaemonSets
Operators replace the kubelet on each node
Operators are only for third-party apps, never platform components
scenarios.why: An operator = CustomResourceDefinition (the desired-state API) + controller (the reconcile loop). OpenShift runs its core as Cluster Version Operator-managed operators so upgrades, config changes, and day-2 operations happen declaratively through the API instead of SSH and scripts. The same pattern is available for your own applications via OperatorHub.
scenarios.hint: What watches a custom resource and drives the world toward what it declares?

scenarios.title: IPI or UPI?
scenarios.situation: You're planning an OpenShift install on bare metal with no cloud API. The docs mention installer-provisioned infrastructure (IPI) and user-provisioned infrastructure (UPI).
scenarios.prompt: Which fits, and what's the key difference?
choices: UPI — you provision the machines, networking, DNS, and load balancers yourself; IPI has the installer create infrastructure via a cloud API
IPI — the installer works on any infrastructure including bare metal without a cloud API
They're identical — just two names for the same flow
UPI means Red Hat provisions it for you remotely
scenarios.why: IPI = the installer drives a cloud provider API to create VPCs, VMs, DNS, LBs (full automation, needs a supported cloud). UPI = you provide all infrastructure to spec (required for bare metal, restricted networks, unsupported platforms) and the installer only deploys OpenShift onto it. Bare metal with no cloud API means UPI (or the assisted installer, which simplifies UPI).
scenarios.hint: Who creates the VMs — the installer, or you?

scenarios.title: Onboarding a developer to a project
scenarios.situation: Ana joins the team-a project. She needs to deploy and edit resources there — but must NOT get cluster-wide powers.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct grant?
choices: oc adm policy add-role-to-user edit ana -n team-a — project-scoped edit role
oc adm policy add-cluster-role-to-user cluster-admin ana — simplest
oc adm policy add-role-to-user admin ana — without -n it applies everywhere
Give Ana the kubeadmin password — fastest onboarding
scenarios.why: OpenShift RBAC: 'oc adm policy add-role-to-user <role> <user> -n <project>' binds a namespaced Role (edit = full access within the project except RBAC/quota admin) to the user in that project only. ClusterRoleBindings (cluster-admin) are cluster-wide — never for routine onboarding. '-n' scoping is the whole point.
scenarios.hint: Which flag keeps the grant inside one project?

scenarios.title: Blocked by the SCC
scenarios.situation: A Pod fails to create: 'unable to validate against any security context constraint'. The container runs as root and wants hostPath access.
scenarios.prompt: What is happening, and what is the right fix?
choices: No SCC admits the Pod's security context — fix the Pod (run as non-root, drop hostPath) rather than granting privileged SCC
Add the anyuid SCC to the service account immediately
SCCs are advisory — the Pod will start after a few retries
Delete the SCCs — they're incompatible with Kubernetes
scenarios.why: SCCs are admission controllers: a Pod must be admittable by at least one SCC available to its service account. 'restricted' (the default) forbids root, hostPath, privileged. The right fix is almost always to make the workload compliant (arbitrary UID, no host access). Granting 'privileged' or 'anyuid' SCCs is a security exception needing justification — never the first move.
scenarios.hint: Should you change the workload or weaken the guardrail?

scenarios.title: One team ate the cluster
scenarios.situation: Team-b deployed 200 replicas and starved other projects. You need per-project CPU/memory caps and per-container defaults.
scenarios.prompt: Which two objects do this?
choices: ResourceQuota (project-wide caps) plus LimitRange (default/min/max per container) — apply both in each project
ClusterResourceQuota only — project quotas don't exist
ResourceQuota alone — it also sets container defaults
LimitRange alone — it caps project totals
scenarios.why: ResourceQuota caps aggregates per project (e.g., requests.cpu: 20, pods: 50) and rejects creations that would exceed them. LimitRange sets defaults and min/max per Pod/container so every container gets sane requests/limits. Together they give fair sharing; ClusterResourceQuota extends this across multiple projects for admin-level multi-tenancy.
scenarios.hint: Which object caps totals, and which sets per-container defaults?

scenarios.title: CI needs to deploy
scenarios.situation: Your CI pipeline must 'oc apply' into the staging project. Using a human user's credentials in CI is banned.
scenarios.prompt: What is the OpenShift-native approach?
choices: Create a ServiceAccount in staging, grant it the edit role, and give CI its token — scoped, rotatable, auditable
Share the kubeadmin credentials with CI — it's automated so it's safe
Create a human user 'ci-bot' with a password in the pipeline
ServiceAccounts are only for Pods — CI must use user accounts
scenarios.why: 'oc create sa ci-deployer -n staging' + 'oc adm policy add-role-to-user edit system:serviceaccount:staging:ci-deployer -n staging'. The SA token (a Secret or TokenRequest) goes to CI. It's scoped to one project, doesn't expire with employee offboarding, and its actions audit as the SA — unlike shared human creds.
scenarios.hint: What non-human identity exists precisely for workloads and automation?

scenarios.title: Managing 40 developers
scenarios.situation: Forty developers across 4 teams need project access. Binding each user individually is already unmanageable.
scenarios.prompt: How do you scale RBAC?
choices: Create Groups per team ('oc adm groups new team-a'), bind roles to groups, and sync membership from LDAP/IdP
Give everyone cluster-admin — teams are trusted
One shared 'dev' user per team with the password in chat
RBAC can't use groups — individual bindings are the only way
scenarios.why: Groups are first-class RBAC subjects: bind 'edit' to group 'team-a' once in the project, then manage membership centrally. 'oc adm groups sync' (or IdP group sync via LDAP/OIDC claims) keeps it automated — joiners/leavers update in one place. Individual bindings don't scale and rot when people leave.
scenarios.hint: What RBAC subject represents many users at once?

scenarios.title: Auditor access
scenarios.situation: An auditor needs to inspect resources in the payments project but must not change anything. Someone suggests the 'edit' role 'since it's read-mostly'.
scenarios.prompt: Which role is correct, and why not edit?
choices: 'view' — read-only on most resources; 'edit' allows creating/deleting workloads, which violates least privilege
'edit' — it's effectively read-only for auditors
'admin' — auditors need to see RBAC bindings too
cluster-admin scoped with -n — namespaces limit cluster roles
scenarios.why: OpenShift's default roles: view (read-only), edit (manage most resources, can't touch RBAC/quotas), admin (project admin incl. RBAC). Least privilege means view for auditors. Note: '-n' doesn't scope a ClusterRoleBinding — that's what makes cluster-admin grants so dangerous.
scenarios.hint: Which default role is read-only by design?

scenarios.title: From git to image, in-cluster
scenarios.situation: You want pushes to the app's git repo to automatically build a container image inside OpenShift — no external CI for this simple service.
scenarios.prompt: Which BuildConfig strategy and trigger do this?
choices: Source strategy (S2I) with a GitHub webhook trigger — code + builder image in, runnable image out, triggered on push
Docker strategy with manual builds — webhooks don't exist for builds
Jenkins Pipeline strategy — the only automated option
BuildConfigs can't pull from git — use a local binary build only
scenarios.why: BuildConfigs support strategies: Source (S2I injects code into a builder image), Docker (Dockerfile build), Custom. Triggers: webhook (GitHub/GitLab push → rebuild), image change (rebuild when base image updates), config change. 'oc start-build' kicks off manual/binary builds. The output pushes to an ImageStream tag.
scenarios.hint: Which strategy combines your source code with a builder image?

scenarios.title: Why not just use image tags?
scenarios.situation: Your Deployment references 'image-registry.openshift-image-registry.svc:5000/team-a/api:latest'. A teammate asks why you don't point at the external registry directly.
scenarios.prompt: What do ImageStreams add?
choices: An ImageStream tracks tags → immutable image digests, triggers redeploys on new images, and abstracts the registry location — 'latest' always resolves to a specific digest
ImageStreams are just DNS aliases — no functional difference
They're required — external registries are blocked
ImageStreams store the image bytes themselves
scenarios.why: An ImageStream is a local named reference: each tag points to a specific image digest, updated when new images push. Deployments referencing the stream get imageChangeTriggers — automatic redeploys on new builds. It decouples workloads from registry URLs and makes 'which exact image is running' auditable via digest.
scenarios.hint: What does the stream resolve a floating tag into?

scenarios.title: Build from local code
scenarios.situation: You're iterating rapidly and don't want to push to git for every test build. You want to build from your working directory.
scenarios.prompt: How?
choices: oc start-build api --from-dir=. (or --from-file) — streams local content to a BuildConfig with a binary source
Binary builds don't exist — commit to git every time
oc apply -f localdir/ — apply builds images
Copy the code into a running Pod and commit the container
scenarios.why: BuildConfigs with binary source accept 'oc start-build <bc> --from-dir=.', --from-file, or --from-archive — uploading local content for the build without a git round-trip. Perfect for inner-loop development. The BuildConfig must exist first (strategy docker or source with binary: {}).
scenarios.hint: Which start-build flag uploads your working directory?

scenarios.title: The build that never stops
scenarios.situation: Every completed build triggers another build, infinitely. The BuildConfig has an image change trigger on the output ImageStream tag.
scenarios.prompt: What caused the loop, and how do you break it?
choices: The output tag triggers its own input — point the imageChange trigger at the BASE image stream, not the output, or disable the trigger
Webhooks fire twice — delete the webhook
Builds always loop — this is expected
The registry is echoing pushes — restart it
scenarios.why: Image change triggers fire when the watched ImageStreamTag updates. If the BuildConfig watches its own output tag, each successful build updates the tag → triggers another build. Fix: trigger on the builder/base image stream (rebuild when the base updates — usually desired) and let the output tag update silently, or set the trigger to manual.
scenarios.hint: What updates as a result of the build — and what is watching that update?

scenarios.title: Customizing the S2I build
scenarios.situation: The default S2I builder image almost fits, but you need to run database migrations during the build and set custom environment variables.
scenarios.prompt: How do you customize a Source build without forking the builder?
choices: Add .s2i/bin/assemble and .s2i/bin/run scripts in your repo to override/extend build and run behavior, plus .s2i/environment for env vars
S2I can't be customized — write a Dockerfile instead
Edit the builder image in the registry directly
Environment variables aren't supported in S2I
scenarios.why: S2I looks for .s2i/bin/assemble (build) and .s2i/bin/run (runtime) in your source to override the builder's defaults, and .s2i/environment for build-time env vars. This keeps you on the supported builder image while customizing the steps — the middle path between stock S2I and a full Dockerfile strategy.
scenarios.hint: Where in your repo can you drop scripts that override the builder's defaults?

scenarios.title: Pulling from the external registry
scenarios.situation: Your BuildConfig needs a base image from a private external registry. Builds fail with 'unauthorized'.
scenarios.prompt: How do you give builds registry credentials?
choices: Create a dockerconfigjson Secret and link it to the builder ServiceAccount ('oc secrets link builder mysecret --for=pull')
Put the password in the BuildConfig YAML — it's base64'd
docker login on every node manually
Private base images aren't supported — mirror publicly
scenarios.why: 'oc create secret docker-registry' makes the credential Secret; linking it to the 'builder' SA with --for=pull attaches it to build Pods' imagePullSecrets. (--for=mount is for pushing.) The integrated registry is pre-authenticated; external private registries need this wiring for both builds and deployments (link to 'default' SA for runtime pulls).
scenarios.hint: Which ServiceAccount runs build Pods, and how do pull secrets attach to it?

scenarios.title: Exposing the service
scenarios.situation: Your 'api' Service (port 8080) works in-cluster. You need it at https://api.apps.cluster.example.com with TLS.
scenarios.prompt: What is the minimal path, and what TLS mode terminates at the router?
choices: oc expose svc/api --hostname=api.apps.cluster.example.com, then add edge TLS termination — router decrypts, re-encrypts or forwards HTTP to the Pod
oc expose creates HTTP only — TLS needs a separate Ingress
Change the Service to LoadBalancer — Routes can't do TLS
TLS is automatic on all Routes — no configuration needed
scenarios.why: 'oc expose svc/<name>' creates a Route with an admitted hostname. TLS modes: edge (router terminates TLS, traffic to Pod is HTTP), passthrough (router passes TLS through to the Pod — Pod terminates), re-encrypt (router terminates then re-encrypts to the Pod). Edge is the common default; choose per security needs. Certificates via 'oc create route ... --cert/--key' or the console.
scenarios.hint: Where can TLS terminate — at the router, at the Pod, or both?

scenarios.title: Two routers, two tenants
scenarios.situation: Tenant A's routes must be served by router-shard-a, tenant B's by router-shard-b, for compliance isolation.
scenarios.prompt: How do you steer Routes to specific routers?
choices: Route labels + router shard selection (namespace or route-label selectors on the IngressController) — each shard serves only matching Routes
Routes can't be assigned — one router serves all
Create two clusters — sharding isn't supported
DNS round-robin — traffic splits naturally
scenarios.why: OpenShift supports multiple IngressControllers (router shards), each with namespaceSelector or routeSelector choosing which Routes/namespaces it serves. Label tenant Routes accordingly. This gives compliance isolation, per-shard tuning, and internal vs external router separation (the default internal/external pattern).
scenarios.hint: What selects which Routes a given router serves?

scenarios.title: The Pod with a changing IP
scenarios.situation: A partner firewall allows only one fixed source IP for your cluster's outbound API calls, but Pod IPs change constantly.
scenarios.prompt: How do you present a stable egress IP?
choices: EgressIP — assign a fixed IP from a reserved pool to a namespace's (or Pod's) outbound traffic via the OVN-Kubernetes egress IP feature
Use the node's IP — Pod traffic always SNATs to the node IP
Egress IPs must be configured per Pod manually
Outbound IPs can't be stabilized — ask the partner to allow the whole Pod CIDR
scenarios.why: EgressIP allocates stable IPs from an admin-reserved pool to namespaces/Pods; outbound traffic from those workloads SNATs to the EgressIP (hosted on a chosen node, with failover). It's the answer for partner allowlists and compliance. Related: EgressFirewall for L3/L4 outbound rules per project. (Default OVN-Kubernetes networking in modern OpenShift.)
scenarios.hint: What gives a namespace's outbound traffic a fixed source address?

scenarios.title: Internal TLS without cert-manager
scenarios.situation: Your api Service needs serving TLS certs for in-cluster clients. You don't want to run a full CA.
scenarios.prompt: What does OpenShift provide natively?
choices: The service CA — annotate the Service with service.beta.openshift.io/serving-cert-secret-name and OpenShift issues and rotates a cert signed by the cluster's service CA
Internal TLS isn't possible — only Routes get certs
Use the router's default cert for Services too
Generate self-signed certs and bake them into the image
scenarios.why: OpenShift runs an internal service CA: annotating a Service auto-provisions a Secret with a serving certificate (rotated automatically), and the CA bundle is injectable into client Pods via the service-ca ConfigMap annotation. It covers service-to-service TLS with zero CA operations — distinct from Route (edge) certs.
scenarios.hint: Which annotation makes the platform mint a serving cert for a Service?

scenarios.title: Default-deny for the project
scenarios.situation: The payments project must deny all Pod-to-Pod traffic by default, then allow only api→db on 5432.
scenarios.prompt: What is the two-policy pattern?
choices: A default-deny policy (podSelector: {} with no ingress/egress rules) plus an allow policy selecting db Pods permitting ingress from api Pods on port 5432
One policy is enough — deny and allow can't coexist
NetworkPolicies default to deny — no policy needed
Use a Route — it firewalls Pod traffic
scenarios.why: Kubernetes is allow-all by default; an empty-ingress policy (podSelector: {} ) flips the project to default-deny. Then additive allow policies whitelist required flows (api podSelector → db podSelector, port 5432). Policies are additive (union of allows) — deny is only via absence of allows. OVN-Kubernetes enforces them in OpenShift.
scenarios.hint: How do you express 'deny everything, then allow this' with additive policies?

scenarios.title: End-to-end encryption requirement
scenarios.situation: Compliance requires TLS encryption all the way to the application Pod — the router must NOT decrypt traffic.
scenarios.prompt: Which Route TLS mode, and what must the Pod do?
choices: Passthrough — the router forwards TLS bytes untouched; the Pod (app) must terminate TLS itself with its own certificate
Edge — the router decrypts but promises not to look
Re-encrypt — the router decrypts and re-encrypts, which satisfies 'no decryption'
Routes can't do this — use NodePort
scenarios.why: Passthrough: the router uses SNI to route without decrypting — the app Pod terminates TLS (needs the cert + TLS-speaking app). Edge decrypts at the router (Pod gets HTTP). Re-encrypt decrypts at router then re-encrypts to the Pod (Pod needs a cert, often the service CA one). Only passthrough keeps the router blind — at the cost of no L7 routing/inspection.
scenarios.hint: Which mode never gives the router the plaintext?

scenarios.title: What an operator actually is
scenarios.situation: You're asked to 'write an operator' for the in-house message queue: it should provision, scale, upgrade, and back up queue clusters from a simple YAML spec.
scenarios.prompt: What are the pieces you build?
choices: A CRD defining the desired state (MessageQueueCluster spec) + a controller implementing the reconcile loop (observe → diff → act), packaged via OLM
A shell script run by cron — that's an operator
A Helm chart — identical to an operator
Operators can't be written in-house — only Red Hat ships them
scenarios.why: Operator = CustomResourceDefinition (your API: spec for desired state, status for observed) + controller (watch the CR, reconcile toward spec: create StatefulSets, handle upgrades, schedule backups). The Operator SDK scaffolds this in Go/Ansible/Helm. Package with a ClusterServiceVersion for OperatorHub/OLM lifecycle (install plans, channels, upgrades).
scenarios.hint: What watches your custom resource and drives reality toward its spec?

scenarios.title: Installing from OperatorHub
scenarios.situation: You need the database operator in namespace 'db'. You want to control WHEN updates apply (not auto-update on release day).
scenarios.prompt: What OLM objects do you create, and which setting gates updates?
choices: An OperatorGroup (target namespaces) + Subscription (channel + source); set installPlanApproval: Manual to approve InstallPlans yourself
Just the CSV — OLM figures out the rest
Subscriptions auto-update always — manual approval doesn't exist
Install the operator YAML with oc apply — OLM is optional
scenarios.why: OLM flow: OperatorGroup scopes the operator to namespace(s) → Subscription (package, channel, source, installPlanApproval) → OLM resolves a ClusterServiceVersion → InstallPlan (auto-applied if Automatic, pending approval if Manual). Channels (stable/fast) choose the update stream. Manual approval = change control for production operators.
scenarios.hint: Which Subscription field makes updates wait for your approval?

scenarios.title: CSV stuck in Pending
scenarios.situation: Your operator's ClusterServiceVersion sits in 'Pending' phase. The InstallPlan is approved. Nothing is installed.
scenarios.prompt: What are the common causes to check?
choices: Unmet requirements (missing CRDs/APIs), RBAC/permission errors, OperatorGroup targeting mismatches, or conflicting installed operators — check CSV status conditions and events
CSVs always take 24 hours — wait
Delete the namespace — Pending means corrupted
Pending is the running state — it's fine
scenarios.why: CSV phases: Pending → InstallReady → Succeeded (or Failed). Pending usually means OLM can't satisfy requirements: required CRDs not present, insufficient RBAC, no matching OperatorGroup, or version conflicts. 'oc describe csv' conditions + events name the blocker. This is the standard OLM debug path.
scenarios.hint: What does the CSV's status conditions say it's waiting for?

scenarios.title: The operator that owns the nodes
scenarios.situation: A teammate asks for a concrete example of 'day-2 operations via operator' on the platform itself.
scenarios.prompt: Which platform operator best illustrates it?
choices: The Machine Config Operator — declaratively manages OS config (files, systemd units, kernel args) across node pools with controlled drain/reboot rollouts
The web console operator — it only serves the UI
Operators don't manage the platform — only apps
The scheduler — it's technically an operator
scenarios.why: MCO is the canonical platform operator: MachineConfig CRs declare node desired-state; the controller renders, applies, drains, and reboots nodes pool by pool — upgrades, config changes, and drift correction as reconciliation. Same pattern as etcd/cluster-version operators. It demonstrates operators encoding operational knowledge (safe rollout sequencing) as software.
scenarios.hint: Which operator rolls out OS changes with drain-and-reboot sequencing?

scenarios.title: Operator or Helm chart?
scenarios.situation: You're packaging the message queue. Helm chart exists; someone proposes an operator instead. The queue needs automated failover, version upgrades, and scheduled backups.
scenarios.prompt: When does the operator earn its complexity over Helm?
choices: When ongoing lifecycle automation (failover, upgrades, backups) must run continuously — Helm renders install-time manifests; operators reconcile runtime state in a loop
Always — operators replace Helm entirely
Never — Helm can do everything operators do
Operators are only for Red Hat products
scenarios.why: Helm = package manager (template + install/upgrade/rollback at deploy time). Operator = running controller (continuous reconcile: detect failed primary → promote replica, run upgrade steps in order, schedule backups). The Operator SDK even has a Helm-based operator type for the middle ground. Choose by lifecycle needs: one-shot deploy → Helm; ongoing automation → operator.
scenarios.hint: What happens after install — who keeps watching the queue?

scenarios.title: Which channel?
scenarios.situation: The database operator offers channels 'stable', 'fast', and 'candidate'. Production needs predictability; dev wants the newest features.
scenarios.prompt: How do you choose?
choices: Production pins 'stable' (vetted releases); dev can track 'fast' — channels are update streams, and you can move between them deliberately
Always use 'candidate' — newest is best everywhere
Channels are cosmetic — they all serve the same CSV
One channel per cluster — you can't mix
scenarios.why: Channels are OLM's release streams per package: stable (vetted), fast (newer, less baked), candidate (pre-release). Subscriptions pin a channel; moving channels is a deliberate upgrade action. Different namespaces can even track different channels — prod stable, dev fast — giving controlled exposure to new operator versions.
scenarios.hint: What does a channel control about the updates you receive?

scenarios.title: Anatomy of a Tekton pipeline
scenarios.situation: You're moving a Jenkins pipeline to OpenShift Pipelines. You need: clone → test → build image → deploy, sharing the workspace between steps.
scenarios.prompt: What are the Tekton objects, and how do they relate?
choices: Tasks (reusable units: clone, test, build) composed in a Pipeline; PipelineRuns execute it; Workspaces (PVC) share data between Tasks
Pipelines contain Pods directly — Tasks are optional
One TaskRun per pipeline — PipelineRuns don't exist
Workspaces are git repos — PVCs aren't used
scenarios.why: Tekton model: Task = reusable step template (or ClusterTask for shared), Pipeline = DAG of Tasks with params/results wiring, TaskRun/PipelineRun = executions. Workspaces abstract shared storage (volumeClaimTemplate for dynamic PVCs). 'tkn' CLI manages them: tkn pipeline start, tkn pipelinerun logs -f. It's Kubernetes-native CI/CD — everything is a CR.
scenarios.hint: Which object is the reusable template, and which is the execution?

scenarios.title: Git push starts the pipeline
scenarios.situation: You want GitHub pushes to automatically start the PipelineRun with the right revision — no polling, no manual tkn commands.
scenarios.prompt: What are the Trigger objects involved?
choices: EventListener (receives webhook) + TriggerBinding (extracts fields like revision) + TriggerTemplate (renders the PipelineRun) — exposed via a Route
A CronJob polling git — triggers don't exist
Webhooks call tkn directly — no objects needed
Pipelines poll git natively — no webhook needed

Routes: openShift also supports standard Ingress, but Routes predate it and add features like edge/passthrough/re-encrypt TLS termination modes.

concepts: Routes: label tenant Routes accordingly.

lessons.title: OpenShift — Core concepts
concepts: Routes are OpenShift's L7 ingress: the router maps public hostnames to Services with edge, re-encrypt, or passthrough TLS termination — no manual NodePort or node IPs needed.
BuildConfigs turn source into images inside the cluster. S2I (source-to-image) assembles code into a builder image; builds run as arbitrary UIDs, so images must not assume a fixed user or home.

Security Context Constraints are admission control: the restricted SCC (default) forbids root and requires UIDs from the namespace's allocated range. Running as root needs an explicit, narrowly-scoped SCC grant.
Operators extend the cluster via OLM: Subscriptions track channels, InstallPlans stage CSV upgrades (manual approval pauses for human sign-off), and CRDs define the custom APIs.
ImageStreams are local references to image digests; tags pointing at external registries only refresh on `oc import-image` (or scheduled imports) — registry pushes alone don't update the cluster.

example.code:
oc new-project demo
oc new-app https://github.com/example/app.git
oc expose svc/app --hostname=app.apps.cluster.example.com
oc get routes

pitfalls: Common trap: upstream Helm charts that run as root — they fail SCC admission; remove runAsUser: 0 or grant anyuid narrowly.
Common trap: expecting `latest` ImageStreamTags to track registry pushes without import-image or scheduled imports.
Common trap: manual-approval Subscriptions silently stalling upgrades at the InstallPlan.
Common trap: granting anyuid to the default service account broadly instead of the one SA that needs it.

lessons.title: OpenShift Core Concepts — Projects, Builds, Routes
concepts: A Project is OpenShift's namespaced tenancy boundary: `oc new-project` wraps a Kubernetes namespace with additional annotations and resource controls; most `oc` commands operate in the current project context.

BuildConfigs and ImageStreams automate image builds inside the cluster: a BuildConfig (source-to-image, Docker, or pipeline strategy) produces images that land in an ImageStream, and Deployments trigger on ImageStream tag changes.
A Route is OpenShift's Ingress equivalent with first-class TLS: `oc expose svc/api` creates a Route, and edge/reencrypt/passthrough termination modes control where TLS ends.

SecurityContextConstraints (SCCs) are the admission gate: pods are checked against SCCs at admission, and the default `restricted` SCC blocks running as root — the classic cause of 'pod rejected' errors for charts written for vanilla Kubernetes.
The `oc` CLI is kubectl plus OpenShift verbs: `oc new-app`, `oc start-build`, `oc rollout`, and `oc adm policy` cover the PaaS workflows that plain kubectl doesn't.

example.code:
oc new-project shop
oc new-app --name=api https://github.com/acme/api --strategy=source
oc start-build api --follow
oc expose svc/api --hostname=api.example.com
oc get route api -o yaml | grep -A3 tls:
example.walkthrough: Create an isolated project, build from source with S2I, follow the build logs, expose the service through a Route with a custom hostname, and verify the TLS termination settings. This is the core OpenShift deploy loop.

pitfalls: Common trap: applying vanilla Kubernetes YAML that runs as root — the restricted SCC rejects it; set runAsNonRoot / drop capabilities or request the right SCC.
Common trap: expecting an Ingress controller — OpenShift uses Routes; an Ingress object without the ingress controller configured does nothing.
Common trap: `oc expose` on the wrong Service port — the Route targets the Service port, not the container port; check `oc describe svc` first.
Common trap: ImageStream tag drift — `:latest` in an ImageStream follows new builds; pin tags or trigger policies when you need immutable deploys.
